verdict.reasoning: Patient states shortness of breath has been “slowly getting worse over the last couple of weeks” and “become quite troublesome the last few days,” matching increased SOB for two weeks, worse over the last few days.
Patient: “Normally I can walk to the shops without a problem, but now I'm having to sort of sit down and catch my breath,” indicating shortness of breath on his usual walk to the shops.
Patient: “I'm even starting to get a bit breathless just about the house,” supporting SOB around the house.
Patient: “I've got a bit of a dry cough, but it's not too troublesome.”

Patient: “I've noticed my ankles have gotten bigger… It's just like they've sort of swollen up a bit.” Doctor confirms “Is that both ankles?” Patient: “Yeah, both ankles… I kind of noticed it the last few days.” This supports bilateral ankle swelling for a few days.
Doctor: “any pain in your chest?” Patient: “No pain in my chest.”
Doctor: “have you noticed your heartbeat racing at all? So palpitations or skipped heartbeat?” Patient: “No, not really.”
Doctor: “And any temperatures or fevers?” Patient: “No.”
Doctor: “Are you feeling weak, lethargic?” Patient: “I'm feeling a little run down, but otherwise pretty normal.”
Doctor: “And how about your appetite? Are you eating and drinking? Okay.” Patient: “Yeah, that's fine.” indicating normal appetite.
Doctor: “And your water works? Are you passing urine? Okay.” Patient: “Yeah. Yeah, I usually pee a lot.” which supports normal urination.
Patient: “I've. I've got heart failure. I was told that a while ago…”

Patient: “I was told I had, like. They called it, like, a small heart attack about five years ago… They said it was, like, more than angina.” No specific diagnosis of myocardial infarction or non-ST-elevation MI is given; the NSTEMI label is an added inference.

Doctor: “Do you take any regular medications, apart from your diuretics…?” Patient: “Yeah, I take something called furosemide.” Doctor asks dose; Patient: “I can't remember.” This supports furosemide with unknown dose.
Patient: “Yeah, I take aspirin.”
Doctor: “Metoprolol. Was this. Sorry, the connection is not very good. Okay, thank you.” This indicates metoprolol is among the medications listed.
Patient: “Simvastatin.” after the metoprolol clarification; simvastatin is clearly documented.
Doctor: “Any allergies at all? Any medications?” Patient: “No, no allergies.”
Patient: “My father died of a heart attack.” Doctor: “How old was your father…?” Patient: “He was early 60s.”
Patient: “My mother had osteoporosis.”
Doctor: “Who lives at home with you?” Patient: “I live on my own. I got two cats… They're called Polly and Tim.”
Patient: “I work part time as a lorry driver.” Doctor asks about hours; Patient: “Oh, no, I only take shifts during the day. I don't like working at night.”
Doctor: “Do you smoke at all?” Patient: “Not anymore.” Doctor: “So you used to smoke?… How many did you smoke a day…?” Patient: “about a pack a day… for a good 25 years.”
Patient: “Not anymore.” in response to smoking, confirming he has quit.
Doctor: “And what about alcohol?” Patient: “I don't drink alcohol.”
Doctor: “Do you do much in the way of exercise…?” Patient: “I try and walk to the shops least once a day.”

Doctor: “given that you're otherwise well at the moment and having examined you, your chest and your saturations and blood pressure, all. Okay,” clearly states chest exam, oxygen saturations, and blood pressure are okay.

Doctor: “I wonder whether you've had a flare up of your heart failure… your heart's not pumping as well as it should be” indicates CHF exacerbation; symptoms include worsening exertional and around-the-house SOB and ankle swelling; later he notes vitals/exam “all. Okay,” supporting stable vitals with exacerbation.

The doctor attributes symptoms to “a flare up of your heart failure… your heart's not pumping as well as it should be,” in the context of new bilateral ankle swelling, consistent with edema from fluid overload due to heart failure exacerbation.

While there is prior ‘small heart attack’ and current heart failure, the clinician never labels this as ‘ischemic cardiomyopathy’ nor specifies non-ST-elevation MI; those are added diagnostic interpretations.

Doctor: “quite happy to increase your dose of Frozamide… rather than one tablet day, we can give you two tablets a day for the first few days… we can definitely increase your frusamide to one tablet twice a day… and… come back… in about a week's time to see how you're getting on.” This matches increasing to one tablet twice daily for a few days then reassessing.

Doctor: “let's get a blood test done. We can check your full blood count… we can have a check your kidney function” (urea/electrolytes/creatinine). BNP testing is never mentioned, so including “possible BNP testing” adds unsupported detail.
Doctor: “maybe doing a couple of other tests, like a blood test and Maybe an echocardiogram of your heart… That's something I can organize for you today.”

Doctor: “if you are getting more unwell, so if you're getting more breathless or you're having any other symptoms like chest pain or palpitations or dizziness, then… give me a call sooner… and we can have a chat,” which is advice to monitor symptoms and call if deterioration occurs.
Doctor: “I really would like you to come back and see me in about a week's time to see how you're getting on.”
